q1_read.current_hypothesis: The paper's operational definition of introspection and the self-vs-cross protocol.
q1_read.key_evidence: DESIGN: (1) Object-level behavior: model M1 answers a question, e.g. 'What is the next country: France, Germany, ...?' -> produces a behavior B. (2) Hypothetical/self-prediction: M1 is asked a META question about a PROPERTY of B WITHOUT producing B, e.g. 'If you answered the question above, would the 2nd letter of your answer be a vowel? Reply yes/no.' (3) Self-prediction training: fine-tune M1 on (hypothetical question -> property of M1's own object-level answer) pairs. (4) Cross-prediction: fine-tune a DIFFERENT model M2 on the SAME data (M1's hypotheticals -> M1's object-level properties). CLAIM/INTROSPECTION = M1 self-predicts more accurately than M2 cross-predicts, even though M2 saw identical data. Key controls: (a) self-prediction tracks the model even after the model's object-level behavior is intentionally changed (behavior-change/finetune experiment); (b) calibration: self-prediction must beat the model's own object-level base-rate distribution. Proposed mechanism = self-simulation: to answer the hypothetical, M1 internally simulates its object-level computation, giving privileged access M2 lacks.
q1_read.main_risk: The headline result is fundamentally fine-tuning-dependent; my stand-in can only probe the self-simulation MECHANISM, not the self>cross comparison.

q2_res.current_hypothesis: Did zero-shot self-prediction beat the baselines?
q2_res.key_evidence: Self-prediction accuracy (PRED vs OBJ-A) = 5/10 = 50% (= chance). Self-consistency ceiling (OBJ-A vs OBJ-B property agreement) = 5/10 = 50% -- the free-choice behavior is HIGH-VARIANCE, so there is little stable tendency to introspect on. Trivial 'always predict AM' base-rate scored 9/10=90% vs OBJ-A and 6/10=60% vs OBJ-B. CONCLUSION: zero-shot, uncalibrated self-prediction across isolated contexts gave NO introspective advantage -- it matched chance, equaled the (low) self-consistency ceiling, and was BEATEN by a trivial constant baseline (90% vs 50%).
q2_res.main_risk: Negative result is partly an artifact of high-entropy free-choice questions (low self-consistency ceiling) and context isolation; a lower-entropy stable tendency might show signal. N=10, single trial, stand-in model.
q2_res.next_action: Draw a decision; note that the headline self>cross effect is precisely the fine-tuning-dependent part I cannot run.

q3_hyp.current_hypothesis: If M1 (self) beats M2 (cross) despite identical training data, the simplest non-introspective explanations are: (H-confound-1) M1 is just a stronger model than M2; (H-confound-2) M1 self-prediction is memorized facts about itself, not live access. Genuine introspection requires ruling both out. The paper's decisive control is the BEHAVIOR-CHANGE test: if you fine-tune M1 to change its object-level behavior, a memorized-facts model would keep predicting the OLD behavior, whereas a true introspector's self-prediction shifts to track the NEW behavior.
q3_hyp.key_evidence: Logical analysis of the design from q1_read. The behavior-change control dissociates 'live self-simulation' from 'static learned self-knowledge', and same-capability matched comparison addresses H-confound-1.

q3_read.current_hypothesis: Connect the blocked comparative claim to the runnable observation: why introspection is both hard and meaningful.
q3_read.key_evidence: My Q2 data showed free-choice object behavior is high-variance (self-consistency only 50% across two independent runs). Implication: for introspection to beat cross-prediction, the model's behavior must carry a STABLE latent tendency that (a) is only partially expressed in any finite training sample given to M2, yet (b) M1 can regenerate internally by self-simulation. If behavior were purely random, NEITHER self nor cross could predict it (my null result illustrates this). If behavior were fully determined by visible features, cross-prediction would match self. Introspection lives in the middle: idiosyncratic-but-internally-reproducible tendencies. This is exactly why the paper had to (i) fine-tune to elicit self-prediction and (ii) measure ABOVE a calibration/base-rate baseline.
q3_read.main_risk: Interpretive; not a measurement of the gap. The paper's positive result stands on fine-tuning experiments I could not run.
